posts.title: Endgame Gear OP1 8K V2 Review
posts.body:
**White & Dark Frost**

I have used quite a few mice over the years, but the OP1 8K V2 is probably the first one in a while that has made me lose interest in looking for something else. I initially got the White version, but it had an issue, and GenesisPC helped me get it replaced with the Dark Frost. I have stuck with the Dark Frost ever since, which should tell you enough about how much I like this mouse.

\n\n![152983.jpg](assets/posts/1793919283267-inline-152983.jpg)\n\n

Starting with the shape, because that is easily my favourite part.

I have 19×9 cm hands and use a claw-fingertip hybrid grip. The OP1 might look rather small and narrow, but it works exceptionally well for me. I particularly like the sides, as they let me position my fingers freely without the shape dictating where they should go. At the same time, the narrow and rather aggressive profile gives me a very secure, locked in feeling. I get the freedom to adjust my grip while still having enough contact with the mouse to maintain stability.

I also like that I am not entirely dependent on either my palm or fingertips. It is a bit of both. I can use the rear contact for stability while still making adjustments with my fingers. The shorter length and narrow front work particularly well with this, giving me plenty of room for micro adjustments without feeling like I am fighting the shape.

Tracking, flicking, micro adjustments, you name it. I find the OP1 comfortable and easy to control across the board. More importantly, I dont have to keep thinking about where my fingers should be or constantly readjusting my grip. I just pick it up and use it.

I know the shape wont be for everyone, and I would not recommend it based on hand size alone. But for my grip, this is about as good as it gets. It is also the most comfortable mouse I have used, which is probably the biggest reason I keep going back to it.

\n\n![149110.jpg](assets/posts/1793919349666-inline-149110.jpg)\n\n

Moving on to the hardware, EGG has done a pretty damn good job here.

The Kailh GX switches feel fantastic. They are crisp, responsive and have a satisfying actuation. They are light without feeling flimsy, and I particularly like how effortless they are to spam. The click latency implementation is equally impressive. The OP1 has topped the latency and click testing I have seen, and EGG deserves credit for getting this right.

8K polling is one thing, implementing it properly is another. The PAW3950 sensor and polling implementation have been flawless in my experience. I would not go as far as claiming that 8K polling is going to magically transform your aim, but it is nice knowing that you are getting a properly executed implementation rather than another specification thrown onto a product for marketing purposes.

The coating is another highlight. It is genuinely one of the best I have used. Good grip, nice feel and nothing that makes me want to immediately reach for grip tape(Which i genuinely hate). Combined with the shape, it makes the mouse feel very secure in hand.

The stock skates are good too. Nothing particularly exciting to write home about, but that is not necessarily a bad thing. They work well enough, but i ended up replacing them with Magic Ice full skates and Dream Gamer Saturn dot skates.

The cable is pretty good for a wired mouse. Obviously, wireless is convenient, and I am not going to pretend a cable does not exist, but with a proper setup, it is not something I find particularly bothersome. I eventually switched to a ForkyMods cable though, which is a nice little upgrade.

The scroll wheel is good as well. Nice scrolling feel, defined steps and no real complaints. Although, I would not put too much faith in the whole dustproof encoder terminology. All scroll wheels can eventually develop dust related issues. Calling something dustproof is not going to save it from the inevitable.

I have seen quite a bit of criticism directed towards the scroll wheel especially on places like reddit, but personally, I think it is perfectly good enough. It does what I need it to do, and I dont have any particular complaints about it.

Software is simple and does what it needs to. I dont particularly enjoy having to install unnecessarily complicated software just to configure a mouse, so EGG keeping things straightforward is appreciated.

**Conclusion -**

So what I am basically getting at is that the overall package is very good, especially considering the price.

Flawless 8K polling, excellent click latency, great switches, great coating, decent stock skates, a decent cable, a decent scroll wheel, simple software and solid support. There is very little here that feels like a compromise.

But if there is one thing that makes the OP1 special to me, it is the shape(I know i might be parroting alot about the shape, but years of trying different shapes and finally finding your holy grail has that effect). All the specifications in the world would not mean much if I did not enjoy actually using the thing this much. As the community says = **Shape is King.**

Of course, shape is subjective, and I would not recommend it blindly to everyone. But if it works for your grip, I genuinely think it is one of the best options out there.

For me, it is easily the most comfortable mouse I have used. And at this point, I dont really see a reason to look elsewhere.

posts.title: Endgame Gear Op1 8K V2 Modding Guide
posts.body:
There are quite a few ways to customise the OP1, should you feel the need to.

**Cable -**
If you are looking to replace the stock cable, you have a few options. ForkyMods and PMM Flexcord are worth considering.

ForkyMods cables are custom orders, so you will have to get in touch with the owner directly through Discord (username - 4qg) or you can find him on the official Endgame Gear discord server. The downside is the delivery time, which can be quite long, especially if you are outside Europe.

I would personally avoid the Midori cable. They have a reputation for being prone to breaking and I dont think they are worth the gamble.

Another option is a Hevitas cable from Taobao, GooFish/Xianyu. It is a cheaper alternative that still gets the job done, so worth looking into if you dont want to spend too much on a cable.

Alternatively, you can braid the stock cable yourself, following the method shown by Viscose in one of their videos.


![153101.jpg](assets/posts/1793924906151-inline-153101.jpg)


**Bungee -**
VAXEE Oryza
Zowie Camade II
Razer Mouse Bungee
You can try other bungees as well.

**Base -**
You can either 3D print your own base or buy one. There are both free and paid files available online, but dont just send a file to a print shop and call it a day. The printing material, orientation and settings matter if you want a decent result.(I am speaking from personal experience after a failed attempt)

ForkyMods also offers a base, particularly worth considering if you are using a glasspad. However, I would not recommend it for clothpad users.

There are cheaper alternatives on Taobao and GooFish as well. Just be careful when buying files or printed bases, since some sellers are selling stolen designs. Make sure you are buying from a legitimate seller.


![152965.jpg](assets/posts/1793924951771-inline-152965.jpg)


**Scroll Wheel -**
The ForkyMods scroll wheel is optional. Personally, I dont think it makes a particularly meaningful difference over the stock wheel and saving 1.3 grams is not exactly going to change your life.

If you do want to replace it, though, ForkyMods is probably the cheapest and best option. I would not recommend the expensive option from PMM.

**Shell Mods -**
Complete shell modding is optional too. There are quite a few routes you can take, ranging from PMM kits to custom lightweight body kits. You can also find fingertip oriented shells on GooFish/Xianyu.

I would look into these only if you have a specific reason to change the shape or reduce the weight. There is little point in spending money to modify something that already works perfectly well for you.


![152964.jpg](assets/posts/1793925013169-inline-152964.jpg)


**GX-Compatible Switches -**

**Kailh -**
GX (80M) - Stock Reference. 50-55gf. Balanced tactility, medium click force, high spammability. Verified OP1 GX Mode compatible.

White Sword/Blade - High tactility with a snappy, stiff rebound profile.

**Huano -**
Trasparent White shell, white dot - Standard mechanical 3-pin setup.

Transparent Purple shell, white dot - Soft end/cushion feel, highly spammable.

Transparent Green shell, white dot - Middle-ground tactile response.

Transparent Yellow shell, white dot - Snappy and stiff actuation.

Transparent Blue shell, red dot - Middle-ground feel; direct upgrade over pink dot.

Transparent Blue shell, pink dot - 55-60gf (BSPD 80m). Crisp tactile bump.

Black shell, blue dot - Fast rebound and poppy tactile profile.

Black shell, pink dot - Fast rebound with a crisp tactile snap.

Black shell, red dot - Fast rebound and poppy tactile profile.

Black shell, white dot - Standard mechanical tactile snap.

Blue shell, pink dot - Standard mechanical 3-pin setup.

Blue shell, white dot - Snappy/stiff actuation.

Blue shell, blue dot - Snappy/stiff actuation.

**HNCHK -**
Transparent Black shell, purple plunger (150M) - 60-70gf. High click force and high tactility. Verified OP1 GX Mode compatible.

Transparent Purple shell, purple dot - Standard 3-pin mechanical setup.

Transparent Purple shell, green dot - Assumption/Highly likely compatible.

Transparent Orange shell, orange dot - Assumption/Highly likely compatible.

**Zippy -**
P1 Orange dot (EGG Orange Dot) - Fast spring return with a poppy click profile.

P1 White dot (DF3-P1) - Fast rebound and high spammability.

P1 Blue dot (DF3-P1L0 5M) - 50-80gf. Medium click force, medium tactility, high spammability. Verified OP1 GX Mode compatible.

**Omron -**
D2F-01F - Extremely crisp, low-force feel (~50-60g). Requires swapping to a D2FC top housing/plunger to correct the taller Japanese housing height and prevent shell binding.

D2F-F-3-7 - Distinct click feel; keep standard Japanese housing height considerations in mind.

**Cherry -**
DG2 - Standard mechanical 3-pin setup.

**TTC -**
Gold 30M - Standard mechanical 3-pin setup.

Gold 60M - Standard mechanical 3-pin setup.

Gold 80M - Higher lifespan rating; stiffer leaf tension.

Gold 100M (marketed as 1HM) - Distinct, crisp metallic snap.

**C&K -**
ZMA030 - Lightest consistently available switch (~45-50gf). Its taller plastic actuator may require slight sanding to achieve proper shell clearance. This is an irreversible modification, so proceed carefully.

**Note -**
One thing worth mentioning is that the newer Pink Raw Input version comes with a hotswap PCB and EGG's own selection of switches. This makes experimenting with different switches considerably easier, without having to worry about manually desoldering and soldering them every time.

**Switch Compatibility -**
When using loose mechanical microswitches from the compatibility list, you will need a dedicated hotswap PCB for solderless, plug and play installation. This includes the official Endgame Gear Universal Switch PCBs and compatible aftermarket socketed boards.

**Warning-** Not all switches have pins of exactly the same thickness. If the pins are too thick, dont force them into the sockets. You could end up widening or damaging the contacts, which might make thinner pins sit loosely afterwards. Check the fit before pushing anything in.

The standard OP1 switch modules come with factory soldered switches, so you can't simply drop loose switches into the stock daughterboards. You will need to desolder the existing switches and solder the replacements manually if you are not using a hotswap PCB.

While the switches listed share a standard 3-pin physical layout, that does not necessarily mean every switch will be a perfect drop in fit. Depending on your particular build, minor adjustments may be required. For example, lightly sanding down the top plunger stem on the C&K ZMA030 or swapping the top housing on the Omron D2F-01F may be necessary to achieve proper shell clearance and pre travel spacing.


![152961.jpg](assets/posts/1793925163623-inline-152961.jpg)


**Final Thoughts -**
The OP1 shape is definitely an acquired taste. Not everyone is going to be willing to put up with its narrow profile and relatively small size. And once you start getting into cables, bungees and all the additional modifications, the investment can add up rather quickly.

That said, none of this is necessary. The OP1 is perfectly fine in its stock configuration. Dont feel the need to throw money at modifications just because they are available. There is a difference between improving something and modifying it for the sake of modifying it.

Personally, I consider the OP1 my benchmark for what a mouse should be. In my opinion, it is the best mouse ever produced. Obviously, that is a subjective statement, but I have not come across anything that has made me want to change my mind.

**Credits -**
Switch compatibility & testing data: 4qg/forkymods.com(contact reliability testing and switch feel notes)

Guide & modding content: End(me) - cable, base, scroll wheel, shell modifications and build related information.

posts.title: XENNS Mangird Tea Pro - Not Very Pro
posts.body:
2 Dynamic Drivers + 6 Balanced Armature Drivers | Hybrid Configuration

**359 USD**

Somewhere between what something is supposed to sound like and what it actually sounds like, there is room for a rather considerable disagreement. The Tea Pro is marketed as a balanced IEM with some extra emphasis on the low end for those who enjoy more bassy warm sets. I suppose that is what caught my attention in the first place. I ended up reaching out to a close friend to borrow his unit. I do enjoy a fair bit of bass, but that does not mean I want it getting in the way of everything else. There is only so much you can add before it starts taking away from the music. Unfortunately, I think the Tea Pro crosses that line.

**ACCESSORIES & PRESENTATION -**
![162800.jpg](assets/posts/1794887310185-inline-162800.jpg)

The unboxing experience is pretty good. I like the box and the overall presentation. The accessories are decent enough and I quite like the carrying case. I have no complaints about its colours or practicality either.

The stock cable is perfectly alright in my book. Nothing particularly remarkable, but nothing I feel the need to complain about either. The interchangeable 3.5mm and 4.4mm terminations are a welcome inclusion.

The stock eartips are not particularly impressive either. I would have liked a better selection and I ended up trying a few alternatives instead. I will get into those later.

**BUILD & FIT -**
![162795.jpg](assets/posts/1794887329453-inline-162795.jpg)

The shells are medium-large in size, but the shape seems to work for my ears. They feel solidly built and I have not had any issues with them shifting around or needing constant adjustment. I do start experiencing some discomfort after a couple of hours though.

The faceplate is not particularly appealing to me. It is just not a design I find myself liking, although I suppose that is entirely subjective.

**LOWS -**
The bass is easily my biggest gripe with the Tea Pro. It is excessive, boomy and frankly quite fatiguing. I dont find it particularly controlled either. Rather than adding weight or physicality to the music, it ends up taking over and getting in the way of everything else.

I enjoy a generous low end, so quantity is not inherently an issue for me. I appreciate bass when it is done right. But there is a difference between having a lot of bass and having bass that knows when to get out of the way. The Tea Pro seems to have trouble understanding that distinction.

**Angel - Massive Attack**
Angel is where things become particularly apparent. The bass is an absolute mess. It has a tendency to run wild, dominating the track rather than working alongside it. Quieter elements get buried and even the vocals feel pushed further into the background.

What should be an engaging, almost hypnotic listening experience instead becomes rather exhausting. I find myself paying more attention to the bass than to the track itself and not in a particularly good way.

**MIDS -**
The midrange does not fare much better. The vocals are recessed and while the bass certainly makes matters worse, I dont think it is solely responsible for their placement. The mids feel withdrawn in their own right.

Female vocals are particularly unpleasant. They have this nasal, stuffy quality, almost as though the singer has a cold. There is a certain hoarseness and graininess to them accompanied by a lack of sweetness, openness and expression. They sound rather dull and lifeless when they should be anything but.

**Never Let Go - Hikaru Utada**
Utada's vocals make the problem quite difficult to overlook. There is a stuffiness to the presentation that takes away from the natural character of her voice. Rather than sounding open and expressive, her vocals come across as constrained and lifeless. It is not quite what I want to hear from a track like this.

Male vocals are comparatively better in terms of tonality. They sound reasonably natural, but are still recessed and masked by the bass. So, while their underlying character is less problematic, their placement remains an issue.

Even guitars sound muddy. And this is not limited to one particular instrument or recording. There is a broader issue with how the instruments are reproduced and it takes away from their natural character.

**HIGHS -**
The treble is probably the least offensive part of the tuning, although that is not necessarily a compliment.

It is soft and smooth without any particularly unpleasant peaks or sharpness. However, it also lacks energy, sparkle and extension.

**Zankyosanka - Aimer**
Aimer's vocals and the instrumentation here would normally give me plenty to appreciate, but the Tea Pro does not quite bring the energy I would like. The highs feel subdued, lacking the presence and liveliness that would give the presentation some much needed life.

I dont necessarily need aggressive treble nor am I particularly interested in chasing brightness for the sake of it. But smoothness should not have to come at the expense of engagement. There is a point where being inoffensive starts becoming rather uneventful and the Tea Pro gets a little too comfortable there.

**TECHNICALITIES -**
Detail retrieval is mediocre. Separation and imaging are reasonably fine, so the Tea Pro is not completely devoid of technical ability. However, things get a little messy with more complex arrangements. 

The soundstage leans more towards the intimate side than anything particularly expansive. I find myself wanting a little more width, depth and overall scale. It is not claustrophobic, but neither does it create much of a sense of space around the music. There is nothing particularly noteworthy about its spatial presentation.

The overall presentation feels busy, despite not necessarily being congested. I find it difficult to put my finger on one particular characteristic, but the overall reproduction does not strike me as particularly natural.

**CONCLUDING NOTES -**
![162789.jpg](assets/posts/1794887351926-inline-162789.jpg)

I came away from the Tea Pro feeling disappointed, irritated and, to some extent, confused.

It is not that everything about it is bad. The imaging and separation are fine, the treble is smooth and I quite like the overall packaging. But I just dont enjoy listening to it and that is ultimately where I struggle with the Tea Pro.

I tried different eartips as well. Divinus Velvet in both normal and wide bore, Spinfit W1 and KBEAR Coffee. I was hoping to get something more out of it, but none of them really helped. The sound remained largely the same.

Perhaps the Tea Pro simply is not to my taste. But I would not say I dislike this particular tuning philosophy, nor do I have an issue with bass heavy IEMs. I enjoy a generous low end when it is done well. I just want it to have some control, texture and composure rather than constantly getting in the way of everything else.

For something called the Tea Pro, I suppose I expected a little more refinement. Instead, I got a rather expensive reminder that having more of something does not necessarily make it better.

**SOURCE USED -**
FiiO KA17 - Low and High Gain

posts.title: Softears RSV MK2 - A Wolf in Softer Clothing
posts.body:
5 Balanced Armature Drivers | 4-Way Crossover | Dual Bass Tubes | 4 Independent Acoustic Tubes

**699 USD**

I had rather limited time with the RSV MK2, so this is more of a first impressions piece than a long-term verdict. There are still a few things I would like to explore further, but I think I have spent enough time with it to get a reasonable idea of what it has to offer.

**UNBOXING -**
![162881.jpg](assets/posts/1794895898481-inline-162881.jpg)
The RSV MK2 comes in a rather compact understated black box with an orange accent. Nothing particularly extravagant, but the presentation is neat and everything is laid out quite nicely.

Inside, you get the IEMs, a 6N oxygen-free copper cable with a 4.4mm termination, a 4.4mm to 3.5mm adapter, two sets of eartips (Softears UC and Type-B), a round carrying case, two protective pouches, a cleaning cloth and a cleaning brush.

It is a fairly complete package, with most of what you would expect at this price point. I appreciate the compact packaging too. Not everything needs to arrive in a box large enough to house a small family. There is little to complain about here, at least as far as the accessories are concerned.

**BUILD & FIT -**
![162867.jpg](assets/posts/1794895923237-inline-162867.jpg)
The shells are made of resin with a CNC-machined aluminum faceplate and a carbon fiber V inlay. They are well put together, though I would not call them particularly attention grabbing. Once they are in your ears, there is not much to draw your attention to, which is not necessarily a bad thing. I had no major issues with the fit during my time with them.

**LOWS -**
The bass is one of the more noticeable aspects of this set. It has a good amount of weight to it, with the sub-bass delivering a particularly satisfying impact. The mid-bass has some meat to it as well, but thankfully does not get in the way of everything else. I quite like the balance here. There is enough slam and physicality to make its presence felt without things becoming loose or overdone.

**Otonoke - Creepy Nuts**
R-Shitei's rapid fire delivery and DJ Matsunaga's production make this quite a busy track. There is a lot happening, but the RSV MK2 keeps everything reasonably distinct. The bass has a satisfying fullness and slam to it, while the kick retains plenty of punch when the track gets particularly hectic. I never feel like I am having to work to pick apart what is going on.

**Indigo Night - Tamino**
There is a slow, almost hypnotic quality to this track. Tamino's low wavering voice, the sweeping strings and Colin Greenwood's anchoring bassline give it a rather distinctive atmosphere. I particularly enjoy the way the RSV MK2 handles the latter. There is a good bit of weight to it, but it stays underneath Tamino's vocals. As the track progresses, the arrangement gradually opens up. It is one of those tracks where I find myself paying less attention to individual elements and more to the song as a whole.

**MIDS -**
Vocals are clear and their positioning is pretty much spot on. I usually prefer vocals to sit a little forward, but the RSV MK2 places them more centrally and I actually quite like how they come across here. Male vocals also have a fair bit of warmth to them. There is more body here than I would have expected, especially with the amount of bass on offer.

**Each Time - Tamino**
Tamino moves between his rather intimate lower register and those familiar higher notes. His voice has a satisfying amount of weight in the lower passages, while the higher notes retain that softer, almost fragile quality I enjoy so much. I quite like this contrast, particularly how much his voice changes in character between the two.

**Ref:rain - Aimer**
A slow, melancholic track carried by Aimer's husky, breathy voice. I particularly enjoy the little nuances in her delivery and the RSV MK2 lets those come through quite naturally. There is a nice fullness to her vocals too. They never sound thin or stripped of the character that makes her voice so distinctive.

**HIGHS**
The treble has a little bite to it, but I would not call it particularly aggressive. Some peaks are present, though they have not bothered me much during my time with the RSV MK2. The bass does take some of the brightness out of the overall presentation, but the highs still have plenty of energy. I would not describe this as a dark-sounding set by any means.

**Bi-dama - HACHI**
Bi-dama has a lively digitally driven sound with HACHI's high pitched vocals sitting prominently in the mix. These can become a little intense on brighter sets, but I did not find them particularly troublesome here. The RSV MK2 keeps the presentation energetic without making the vocals uncomfortable to listen to.

**TECHNICALITIES -**
Separation is good and the RSV MK2 has no trouble keeping up with busier arrangements. Clarity and soundstage are decent. Individual elements remain easy enough to follow, even when there is a lot happening. It may not be the most technically impressive set I have heard, but I dont find myself wanting much more in this regard either.

**CONCLUDING NOTES -**
![162874.jpg](assets/posts/1794895947543-inline-162874.jpg)
I quite enjoy this set. The fuller bass presentation is probably my favourite aspect of it, especially considering how well it coexists with the rest of the tuning. There is weight and physicality when the music calls for it, but it does not feel as though everything else has to make room for the bass. That is a balance I appreciate.

The vocals sit a little more centrally than I usually prefer, but I actually quite like how they come across here. All things considered, the RSV MK2 makes for a rather enjoyable listen. I would recommend it to bassheads who enjoy a warmer foundation while still appreciating some brightness, clarity and smoothness up top.

Of course, these are only first impressions. I have not spent nearly enough time with the RSV MK2 to pretend otherwise, so take my conclusions with the appropriate grain of salt.

**SOURCE USED -**
FiiO KA17 - Low and High Gain

**EARTIPS USED -**
Spinfit W1
Eletech Baroque Stage
Softears UC
Lizer Lab Horn SUS

The Horn SUS turned out to be a rather good match for the RSV MK2. I was able to get a good fit, which made quite a difference to the bass presentation. The soundstage also opened up considerably. Quite a fun pairing, actually.

posts.title: Dove Audio SEEDS - Multiple Faces, One Reflection
posts.body:
1 Balanced Armature Driver | 3 Physical Tuning Switches | Multiple Configurations

**69.99 USD**

![158507.jpg](assets/posts/1794912468102-inline-158507.jpg)
Some IEMs are designed with music listening in mind. Others have rather different priorities. The Dove Audio SEEDS falls into the latter category. It is primarily marketed as an FPS gaming IEM and much of its tuning seems to reflect that. Individual sounds are brought out quite deliberately, sometimes at the expense of how naturally everything comes together.

Does that make it a bad music IEM? Not necessarily. There are some genuinely enjoyable configurations here, although getting to them takes a little experimentation. The three physical switches give you quite a few options, but I would not say all of them are equally convincing.

**This one is a bit of a long read, so get comfortable.**

**AESTHETICS, BUILD, FIT & COMFORT -**
![158517.jpg](assets/posts/1794914823521-inline-158517.jpg)
I received the SEEDS as a loaner unit from my dear friend Aswin, so I dont have the retail box or the complete package. I will skip the unboxing and get straight to the IEM.

The shells are made of transparent resin, with the single balanced armature driver visible through the housing. Nothing particularly extravagant, but the three physical tuning switches make the design a little more interesting. They are recessed into the shell and require the supplied tool to operate, so you are unlikely to change settings accidentally.

**Now, about that nozzle.**

At first glance, it looks less like something designed to enter an ear and more like something designed to extract information from one. Calling it a deep-insertion IEM feels like an understatement. I am not sure what they were going for here, but my ear canals certainly were not consulted.

Surprisingly, though, comfort was not much of an issue. I expected the insertion depth to become annoying after a while, but I got along with it rather well. Looks can be deceiving, apparently.

**CABLE & ACCESSORIES -**
![157984.jpg](assets/posts/1794914846550-inline-157984.jpg)
The cable is a bit of an oddity. The ear hooks are not particularly well shaped and dont sit as securely as I would like. The cable itself looks almost like a small LED strip. It works, but I am not sure I would call it attractive.

You also get a USB-C DSP cable with software-based EQ functionality. I have not spent enough time exploring the DSP side of things to comment on what it does to the sound, so I will leave that out of the listening impressions.

The microphone is fairly large for an IEM mic and comes with a physical mute switch. Unfortunately, the switch is rather stiff. It is usable, but not something I would particularly enjoy flicking on and off throughout a gaming session.

The rest of the accessories include a carry box, a pouch for the shells, the switch adjustment tool and five types of eartips: thin red silicone, black silicone, double-flange silicone, dome-shaped foam and cannon-shaped foam tips.

There are also replacement nozzle filters in two varieties. One has a white, donut-shaped opening in the centre, while the other is a solid black circle. The white filter is pre-installed.

**SOUND -**
The SEEDS has three physical switches, which makes experimenting with its tuning a fairly big part of the experience. There are multiple possible combinations.

One thing became apparent fairly quickly: making sounds easier to pick out does not necessarily make music more enjoyable. The SEEDS sometimes does a rather good job of the former while leaving me wanting a little more from the latter.

Some configurations are genuinely enjoyable for music. Others feel more like they are trying to show you where everything is rather than let you enjoy the song. Here is how I got along with them.

**MODE 1 - SWITCH 1 UP, SWITCHES 2 + 3 DOWN**
![163113.jpg](assets/posts/1794915135123-inline-163113.jpg)
**LOWS -**
The bass is very lean here. There is practically no sub-bass rumble and kick drums have little in the way of impact. You can hear them and they are reasonably defined, but there is not much weight behind them.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
This is probably one of the more obvious examples. The bassline is there, as is that little "tuck" sound, but the track is missing much of its usual low end presence. There is very little rumble underneath it. The drums have not disappeared, but the whole thing sounds rather anaemic.

**MIDS -**
Vocals are exceptionally clear and quite exposed. It is almost as though the microphone has been moved closer to the listener. There is not much warmth or body, but I would not necessarily call them thin either.

Instruments are easy to pick out and separation is decent. The problem is that everything feels rather cramped. I can follow individual elements without much trouble, but that does not mean there is much room for them.

**The Offspring - The Kids Aren't Alright**
The guitar distortion and individual string details come through clearly. Drums and vocals are also easy to follow, even when the arrangement gets busy. There is little difficulty picking things apart.

**HIGHS -**
The treble is quite noticeable. Cymbals and smaller details stand out and there is a fair amount of energy up top. It can get a little sharp with certain recordings, though and there is some hiss that becomes apparent with particular vocal passages.

**Lorde - Liability**
The "S" sounds are more prominent than I would like with a little extra hiss that becomes difficult to ignore.

I like the clarity here, but the lack of bass and rather cramped presentation make this a difficult setting to enjoy for everyday listening. It exposes details quite well, but I find myself wanting more weight and substance from the music.

**MODE 2 – SWITCH 2 UP, SWITCHES 1 + 3 DOWN**
![158493.jpg](assets/posts/1794915173069-inline-158493.jpg)
**LOWS -**
The bass is still fairly restrained, but there is a little more of it compared to Mode 1. Dont expect any sudden sub-bass fireworks. There is still very little rumble, although the rhythm section has a bit more presence.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
The bassline is easier to follow this time around. There is still not much physical impact, but it does not sound quite as bare as it did in Mode 1.

**MIDS -**
This is the configuration I keep coming back to.

Vocals are still very clear, but there is a little more body to them. Instruments also have more presence, although they generally sit behind the vocals. I quite like that arrangement. The singer gets your attention, while the accompanying instruments remain easy enough to follow.

Piano notes have a little more weight, guitar picking is easier to notice, and drums are not quite as far in the background. It is not a night and day difference from Mode 1, but the presentation feels more complete.

**Lana Del Rey - Young and Beautiful**
The vocals have an almost angelic quality here. The piano complements them particularly well and I found myself paying more attention to the performance than to the individual sounds. There is something almost hypnotic about it, like the Sirens singing to Odysseus.

**Tamino - Habibi**
Tamino's voice takes centre stage, with the accompanying instruments sitting comfortably behind it. Everything is easy to follow, but the vocal presentation is what draws me in.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
The vocals have a liveliness and forwardness that I particularly enjoy. This is a much more engaging presentation of the track than Mode 1.

**HIGHS -**
Treble extension is quite good. There is a natural shimmer to instruments and details such as violin peaks, acoustic guitar string squeaks and little synth sparkles are easy to hear. Decay also sounds fairly natural.

There is a little bite to sharper vocal sounds, particularly "S", "T" and "Ch", but I did not find it particularly fatiguing. Compared to Mode 1, sibilance is also less obvious in some recordings.

**Tamino - Habibi**
The sharper vocal sounds are noticeably smoother than they were in Mode 1. There is still enough bite to retain their character, but they are no longer quite as distracting.

**Lorde - Liability**
The "S" sounds are still there, but they are less prominent than before. The vocals sound fuller and more natural here and I find myself enjoying Lorde's delivery rather than getting distracted by the occasional sibilant.

This is easily my favourite setting for music. The vocals are lovely, the instruments have enough presence and the treble has a natural quality to it. I dont particularly miss having more bass here either. It is a fairly lean presentation, but one I actually enjoy listening to. I found myself returning to Mode 2 more often than any of the others.

**MODE 3 - SWITCH 3 UP, SWITCHES 1 + 2 DOWN**
![163115.jpg](assets/posts/1794915201349-inline-163115.jpg)
**LOWS -**
The low end is still light, with little sub-bass rumble or physical impact. There is not a huge difference from the earlier lean configurations and bass remains more of a background element than anything else.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
Much like the previous two modes, there's very little rumble. The bassline is audible, but the track still feels rather lightweight.

**MIDS -**
Vocals take a step back here and instruments become more prominent. There is a slightly distant quality to the presentation, with some voices sounding breathier and throatier than they did in Mode 2.

Piano notes also feel more distant, while guitars and drums attract more attention. It is not a massive shift, but it is enough to change where my attention goes when listening.

**The Offspring - The Kids Aren't Alright**
The vocals are a little more recessed, while guitars and drums take up more of the spotlight.

**Tamino - Habibi**
Tamino's voice sounds slightly more distant, with a little more of that throaty, breathy quality. It is not pushed back dramatically, but the difference from Mode 2 is easy to notice.

**Lana Del Rey - Young and Beautiful**
The piano feels more distant and has less weight. The vocals also lose some of that almost angelic quality I liked in Mode 2, although there is still a fair amount of breath and texture.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
The difference from Mode 2 is particularly noticeable here. The vocals lose some of their forwardness and liveliness and I find the track considerably less engaging.

**HIGHS -**
The upper frequencies remain quite noticeable. Guitars and other instrumental details stand out and the lighter balance gives sharper elements a little more room. However, the overall presentation does not feel quite as cohesive as the fuller configurations.

**Lorde - Liability**
The "S" sounds are still audible, although they are not quite as prominent with the vocals sitting further back. The piano also sounds more distant.

Mode 3 is more instrument focused and less intimate than Mode 2. I can see the appeal if you prefer having instruments take the lead, but I personally miss the vocal presence of the previous configuration.

**MODE 4 - SWITCHES 1 + 2 UP, SWITCH 3 DOWN**
![156563.jpg](assets/posts/1794915248448-inline-156563.jpg)
**LOWS -**
Now we are getting somewhere.

There is a noticeable increase in bass presence, with some sub-bass rumble and some much needed impact from kick drums. It is not a basshead presentation, but after the first three modes, the difference is rather obvious.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
The bass finally has some weight behind it. There is rumble underneath the track and the kicks are noticeably louder. The vocals remain clear, while the low end gives everything a much better foundation.

**Creepy Nuts - Otonoke**
The bass is more prominent and punchy and the male vocals have more meat to them. It can occasionally sound a little bloated though.

**MIDS -**
The extra weight is noticeable in the midrange too. Vocals sound fuller and instruments have a more aggressive character. The vocals remain forward, which is something I appreciate.

Piano notes have more weight, while guitars and drums sound considerably more forceful. Some smaller details are not as easy to notice, but there is more substance to the music. It feels less like I am listening to individual elements and more like I am listening to a full arrangement.

**Tamino - Habibi**
Tamino's voice has more weight and body. It is a fuller presentation than the earlier configurations.

**The Offspring - The Kids Aren't Alright**
Guitar riffs and drums sound more aggressive and the vocals have more meat to them. The track has considerably more energy.

**Lorde - Liability**
The piano has more weight and the vocals sound heavier and a little raspier. There is a slight nasal quality, but the voice remains forward and melodic.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
The drums have more weight and the vocals gain some body. The track sounds fuller, although a few of the smaller details are not quite as noticeable.

**HIGHS -**
The treble is still present, but it does not stand out quite as much against the fuller presentation. Sharper elements are less prominent and the hiss I noticed in Mode 1 is considerably less distracting.

**Lorde - Liability**
The vocal hiss is almost gone compared to Mode 1. The voice sounds fuller and less exposed, although there is still a little edge to it.

Mode 4 is a substantial change from the first three configurations. There is more bass, more impact and more body to the vocals. I do miss a little of the smaller detail, but I find this a much more enjoyable presentation overall.

**MODE 5 - SWITCHES 2 + 3 UP, SWITCH 1 DOWN**
![158500.jpg](assets/posts/1794915283921-inline-158500.jpg)
**LOWS -**
There is considerably more slam here. Drums hit harder, bass lines have more weight and the whole thing sounds more aggressive. The downside? Things start getting a little crowded, especially when there is a lot happening at once.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
The rumble is more noticeable and the kicks have considerably more punch. There is a lot more weight behind the rhythm, while the cymbals still retain their shimmer.

**Creepy Nuts - Otonoke**
The opening is punchy and aggressive. The bass has more impact and the track feels considerably more energetic.

**MIDS -**
Vocals are still forward, but they are thicker, raspier and slightly nasal. There is more body to them, although I dont think the extra weight is entirely beneficial.

Separation takes a hit here. Instruments can start bleeding into one another, particularly in busier arrangements. Guitar riffs have plenty of energy, but they dont sound as clean or as clearly separated as they did in Mode 2. There is more meat to everything, but not necessarily more clarity.

**Lorde - Liability**
The piano has more weight and sits prominently in the centre. Vocals are louder and raspier, with a little nasal quality. The "S" sounds are still there, but they aree not particularly prominent.

**Tamino - Habibi**
The voice is louder and thicker, but the guitar starts sounding a little wonky. There is noticeable overlap between the guitar and vocals and separation takes a hit. The piano has more body too, although the notes seem to taper off with a slightly sharp, high pitched edge.

**The Offspring - The Kids Aren't Alright**
Guitars and drums are louder and punchier. The vocals remain forward, and the riffs have more edge and energy. However, some of the finer details are harder to pick out.

**Lana Del Rey - Young and Beautiful**
The piano has more weight and the vocals remain forward and clear in this track. There is more meat to the voice, with that breathy quality still coming through. There is also some bass slam in the background.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
The intro retains its breathy quality and the vocals still sound airy. The drums have more slam, but the presentation feels less delicate than Mode 2.

**HIGHS -**
Treble extension is still good and there is enough energy to keep things lively. However, with everything sounding heavier and more intense, the upper frequencies dont feel quite as cleanly separated from the rest of the mix.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
The upper frequencies are well extended and the breathy elements in the intro are easy to pick out.

Mode 5 is a more aggressive take on Mode 4. There is more slam, more weight and a thicker vocal presentation. Unfortunately, the increased intensity also makes things sound a little crowded, especially with busy tracks. I enjoy the added impact, but I prefer the cleaner presentation of Mode 2.

**MODE 6 - ALL THREE SWITCHES UP**
![158035.jpg](assets/posts/1794915328431-inline-158035.jpg)
**LOWS -**
The low end sounds pretty much the same as Mode 5. There is the same punch, slam and weight and I struggle to find any meaningful difference.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
The bass and kicks are almost identical to Mode 5. Nothing particularly noteworthy changes here.

**MIDS -**
The midrange is very similar too. Vocals retain their body and forwardness, although they seem to sit just a little further back. There is a slight smoothness to them, but it is subtle.

Lorde - Liability
The piano and vocals sound almost identical to Mode 5. The vocals are perhaps a little smoother and less forward, but I would not call it a significant change.

**HIGHS -**
Treble is much the same as Mode 5. There is a slight smoothing in the upper midrange, making things feel a little less aggressive, but the difference is difficult to pin down.

Honestly, I struggle to find much of a difference between these two. The bass sounds pretty much the same and so does everything else. Vocals seem a little smoother and sit slightly further back, but it is subtle. I would not choose Mode 6 over Mode 5 for any particular reason.

**MODE 7 - SWITCHES 1 + 3 UP, SWITCH 2 DOWN**
![156270.jpg](assets/posts/1794915355785-inline-156270.jpg)
**LOWS -**
The low end is fairly restrained again, with more emphasis on definition than physical impact. There is some bass presence, but sub-bass rumble and slam are limited compared to Mode 4. It does have a little more weight than Mode 3, though.

**Massive Attack - Angel**
The bassline is audible with a hint of rumble underneath. The kicks have a defined attack, but they dont carry the same weight as Mode 4.

**Creepy Nuts - Otonoke**
There is enough bass to follow the rhythm, but the opening does not hit with the same punch as the fuller configurations.

**MIDS -**
This is an interesting combination. Instruments retain much of the prominence they had in Mode 3, but vocals gain some of the forwardness found in Mode 4. Neither completely takes over and I find the balance rather interesting.

**Tamino - Habibi**
The guitar has a rather high pitched character, while Tamino's vocals remain smooth and comfortable. They dont have the same sharpness or edge that might be expected from the brighter presentation.

**Lana Del Rey - Young and Beautiful**
Vocals are clear and fairly smooth, although they dont quite have the same angelic quality as Mode 2. The piano also has a little more weight.

**The Offspring - The Kids Aren't Alright**
Guitars and distortion come through clearly. Drums, cymbals and vocals are also easy to follow. There is something about the presentation that almost reminds me of hearing the track in a live room.

**HIGHS -**
The upper frequencies have a noticeable presence, but I would not call the treble particularly sharp. There is enough energy to bring out smaller details and give instruments a defined edge, without consistently becoming harsh or fatiguing.

**Lorde - Liability**
The "S" sounds are noticeable and have a little bite. The piano has some added weight, while the vocals remain clear.

**RADWIMPS - Suzume**
Vocals are forward, with a little brightness around the sharper consonants. Instruments are easy to follow, but the treble itself does not sound particularly sharp.

Mode 7 feels like a mix of Modes 3 and 4. You get some of the instrument focus of Mode 3, with a bit more vocal forwardness and weight from Mode 4. It is an interesting combination, although I still prefer Mode 2 for music.

**GAMING - VALORANT**
Of course, gaming is where the SEEDS is supposed to make the most sense. With Valorant, I am less concerned about bass impact or an expansive soundstage. I want to follow movement, distinguish sounds and work out where someone is coming from, especially when several things are happening at once.

**MODE 4 - SWITCHES 1 + 2 ON**
Mode 4 is my preferred setting here. The presentation feels compact and organised and I find it easier to follow movement and distinguish sounds when there is a lot going on.

What I particularly like is that it does not make every little sound stand out independently. The cues are easy enough to follow, but the overall soundscape still feels coherent. I dont want a collection of isolated noises; I want to understand what is happening around me. Mode 4 does that better than the other configurations I tried.

**MY PICKS -**

Music: Mode 2

Valorant: Mode 4

Those are the two configurations I would keep coming back to. Mode 2 is simply the more enjoyable music setting for me, while Mode 4 makes more sense for gaming.

**CONCLUDING NOTES -**
![158496.jpg](assets/posts/1794915410708-inline-158496.jpg)
I went into the SEEDS expecting an IEM that would prioritise gaming and that is largely what I found. What I did not expect was to enjoy some of its music configurations as much as I did.

Mode 2 is the clear winner for me. The vocals are lovely, instruments are easy to follow and the treble has a natural quality that makes it quite enjoyable. Mode 4 is a good alternative if you want more weight and impact. Mode 5 pushes that further, but the loss of separation becomes difficult to ignore. Mode 6 on the other hand does not offer enough of a change for me to bother switching to it.

For Valorant, Mode 4 is the obvious choice from my testing. Its more organised presentation makes it easier to follow what is happening without turning the soundscape into a collection of disconnected cues.

I would not buy the SEEDS purely for its technical performance nor would I recommend it just because it has three tuning switches. The novelty wears off rather quickly if the configurations themselves are not worth using. Fortunately, there are a few that I genuinely enjoy.

It is not an IEM I woud choose as an all rounder, but I dont think that is necessarily what Dove Audio was going for. There is a decent amount of flexibility here and if you are willing to spend some time experimenting, you might find a configuration that works rather well for you. Just dont expect all seven to be equally worthwhile.
